description:
An ACL rule's `effect` value is a CLOSED set, at every entry point (PROTOCOL_SPEC §6.1.5, spec v1.30.0, #111). `allow` and `deny` are the only legal values — §6.1's field table has always said **MUST** and `schemas/acl-config.schema.json` has always declared the enum — and a rule carrying anything else **MUST** be rejected with `ACLRuleError` naming the rule index and the offending value.

**The entry point is the substance of this fixture, not a detail.** #107 closed the rule KEY set; this closes a legal key's VALUE, and it was found because the check already existed and was reachable from only one of three doors. Drivers **MUST** exercise each door in `entry_points` that the SDK exposes: `load` (an ACL file), `construct` (building the ACL/rule directly in code) and `add_rule` (runtime insertion). §6.1.6 rule 3 is the governing text — accepting a rule through one door while rejecting it at two is worse than either — and an SDK whose `add_rule` returns nothing by its own contract provides a fallible variant beside it or fails loudly in whatever way that language signals an unconstructable value.

`expected_load: ok` means the rule is accepted at every listed door; `reject` means it is rejected at every listed door. There is deliberately no per-door expectation: a value legal through one entry point and illegal through another is the defect, so the fixture cannot have a shape that can express it.

**An unrecognised `effect` MUST NOT be resolved to a decision.** Reading it as `deny` looks safe and is not: under `default_effect: allow` a rule written to permit becomes one that denies everything it matches, and on a `deny` rule the fallback is only accidentally right — correct until someone revisits which way it points. Where a case is rejected there is no access decision to assert, which is the point.

`default_effect` is closed on the same terms. All three SDKs already validated it at every door before v1.30.0, which is what made a rule's `effect` guarding only the file path an internal inconsistency as well as a cross-language one; `default_effect` cases are pinned here so that behaviour stops being correct-by-convention.

test_cases.note: Control: the closed set itself must still be accepted, at every door.

THE DRIVING CASE. `Allow` is what an operator writes by hand, and it is the value that measurably split the SDKs: apcore-python and apcore-typescript rejected it from `ACL.load()` and accepted it through direct construction and `add_rule()`, while apcore-rust rejected it at all three. The value set is closed at EVERY entry point (§6.1.5, §6.1.6 rule 3).
The `deny` side of the same mistake. It must fail for the same reason rather than survive because a non-`allow` string happens to land on the fallback that was already going to deny.
A typo rather than a case error, so no normalisation rule could rescue it.
An empty string is not a shorter way of saying `deny`; it says nothing.

The same rule under `default_effect: allow`, which is where reading an unknown effect as `deny` is visibly WRONG rather than merely silent: the rule the operator wrote to permit would deny everything it matches, flipping those calls with no error. Uses `default_effect: allow` against the house rule deliberately — the damage is not observable against a deny default.

`default_effect` is the same two values one field up, and all three SDKs already rejected an out-of-enum value here at every door before v1.30.0 — which is exactly what made a rule's `effect` guarding only the file path an INTERNAL inconsistency, not merely a cross-language one. Pinned so it stops being correct-by-convention. `add_rule` is not listed: it does not accept a default_effect.
The empty string is not a shorter way of saying `deny`, one field up either.
Control for the pair above: `allow` as a default_effect is legal and must stay loadable. It is the value the house rule warns about (§ ACL default-deny), not an invalid one.
